name: jellyfish
desc: Fast, memory-efficient counting of DNA k-mers
why: Counts DNA k-mers at scale; real bioinformatics you can run on sequence data at home.

brief.what_it_is: Jellyfish is a command-line program for counting k-mers, which are substrings of length k, in DNA sequence. It reads FASTA and multi-FASTA files of DNA sequences and writes its counts in a binary format. You can turn that binary output into human-readable text with "jellyfish dump", or look up specific k-mers with "jellyfish query". The README says it is a C/C++ tool built from source with make and g++.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames k-mer counting as a central step in many DNA sequence analyses and says Jellyfish is meant to do it fast and with little memory. It claims an order of magnitude less memory and an order of magnitude faster than other k-mer counting packages.
brief.how_it_works: The README says Jellyfish uses an efficient encoding of a hash table and exploits the "compare-and-swap" CPU instruction to increase parallelism. The authors' citation describes it as a fast, lock-free approach to parallel k-mer counting. The README does not go into further detail.

brief.install_notes: Debian and Ubuntu: apt install jellyfish. Arch: available from the AUR. FreeBSD: pkg install Jellyfish or build from the ports tree. Windows: the README suggests WSL with a Linux distribution that carries Jellyfish, or Cygwin with a source build. Source build needs make and g++ 4.4 or higher. Building from the git tree also needs autoconf, automake, libtool, gettext, pkg-config and yaggo. Installing into system directories needs sudo and then sudo ldconfig. Language bindings (Ruby, Python, Perl) need SWIG 3 from git and the target language's development files. The README says the bindings are easier to compile from the release tarball.
brief.standout: The speed and memory claims rest on a hash table encoding and compare-and-swap parallelism, which is a lock-free approach rather than the usual locking. It is an established, citable piece of bioinformatics software with a peer-reviewed paper behind it.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a CI workflow badge, and it links to release downloads and packages on apt, AUR and FreeBSD ports, which suggests ongoing packaging. The fetched README gives no release date or last commit date, so I could not confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: No native Windows build; Windows users need Cygwin or WSL. Building from git requires yaggo and several autotools packages. Python, Ruby and Perl bindings need SWIG 3 and extra setup, and the README's Python path example is for python2.7. The README points to doc/Readme.md for usage, which I did not fetch, so I have no flag-level detail beyond dump and query. The README does not state a license in the text I read.

judge.reason: A specialist DNA-analysis tool with a genuinely interesting lock-free, parallel counting design offers a compact way into both genomics and concurrent algorithms.

entry.title: Jellyfish
entry.tldr: Jellyfish counts every substring of length k in DNA sequence files, quickly and with little memory, a basic step in many genome analyses.
entry.deeper_look:
Jellyfish reads FASTA and multi-FASTA files of DNA and counts k-mers: all the substrings of length k that appear in the sequence. It writes the counts in a binary format. `jellyfish dump` turns that into readable text, and `jellyfish query` looks up the count for specific k-mers.

The README describes k-mer counting as a central step in many DNA sequence analyses. Jellyfish exists to make that step cheap. It claims to use "an order of magnitude less memory and an order of magnitude faster than other k-mer counting packages". Those are the authors' claims, backed by a 2011 paper in Bioinformatics.

The technique underneath is the interesting part. The README says it uses an efficient encoding of a hash table and the compare-and-swap CPU instruction to increase parallelism. In other words, many threads update one shared table without taking locks. The brief does not go into more detail than that, but the paper is linked below.

The larger idea is that a genome becomes a frequency table of short words. Counting those words is a way to look at sequence data without aligning it to anything. The brief does not cover the command-line options beyond dump and query, so the project's doc directory is the place to learn the counting step.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the subcommands, including the dump and query commands for reading the binary count files.

entry.whats_unique: It counts k-mers with a lock-free hash table built on compare-and-swap, which is how it keeps memory use and run time low. It is established, citable bioinformatics software with a peer-reviewed paper behind it.
entry.caveats: The brief could not confirm recent activity, and it has no flag-level usage detail, so you will need the doc directory and your own FASTA data to do anything real.
